trendNotes.label: Group 14
trendNotes.essay: Descending from Carbon (C) to Silicon (Si) exhibits the classic inner-core shielding effect. The additional 3s²3p² shell increases the atomic radius significantly (+58%), causing valence electrons to experience a diminished effective nuclear charge (Z_eff). C–C bonds drastically outlast weaker Si–Si bonds. Silicon's network is an intrinsic semiconductor.

trendNotes.label: Group 17
trendNotes.essay: Fluorine to chlorine is the textbook halogen step: both want one electron, but fluorine is a much fiercer oxidizer because it is smaller and more electronegative. Chlorine still disinfects and forms a wide oxo-anion ladder (ClO⁻ to ClO₄⁻) that fluorine barely copies.

trendNotes.label: Group 1
trendNotes.essay: Lithium to sodium keeps the ns¹ pattern, but sodium’s extra shell makes the atom larger and easier to oxidize. Lithium’s small Li⁺ ion polarizes anions and dominates battery electrochemistry; sodium remains the everyday salt cation.

trendNotes.label: Group 18
trendNotes.essay: Neon and argon are both closed-shell gases, but argon is denser and far more abundant in air. Neither forms ordinary molecules; argon’s chemistry, like krypton’s, is a specialist topic, while neon is the lighting benchmark.

discovery.text: Isolated as inflammable air; later named hydrogen by Lavoisier.

elements.history:
In 1766 Henry Cavendish collected a gas from metals and acids and called it inflammable air. He showed that burning it produced water. Antoine Lavoisier later named it hydrogen, from the Greek for water-former, and listed it as an element.

The common isotope, protium, is a single proton. Deuterium was identified in 1931 and tritium in 1934. In 1913 the Balmer lines of hydrogen became the first spectrum explained by Bohr’s model of the atom.

discovery.text: First seen as a solar emission line; later isolated on Earth by Ramsay.

elements.history:
During the 1868 solar eclipse, Pierre Janssen and Norman Lockyer saw a yellow line in the solar spectrum that matched no known element. Lockyer named it helium, from the Greek helios, the Sun. William Ramsay isolated the gas on Earth in 1895 from the uranium mineral cleveite.

Helium stayed a laboratory curiosity until natural-gas wells supplied it in quantity. Below 2.17 K the liquid becomes a superfluid, a discovery of the 1930s that made helium the benchmark quantum liquid.

elements.history:
Johan August Arfwedson found a new alkali in the mineral petalite in 1817, working in Berzelius’s laboratory. Humphry Davy isolated a small amount of the metal by electrolysis soon afterward.

Berzelius named it lithium, from the Greek lithos, stone, because it turned up in rock rather than in plant ash like sodium and potassium. The metal stayed rare until the twentieth century, when its light ion became the working metal of rechargeable batteries.

Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin recognized a new earth in beryl and emerald in 1798. The salts tasted sweet, so the element was first called glucinium. The name beryllium, from the mineral beryl, is the one that lasted. Friedrich Wöhler and Antoine Bussy isolated the metal independently in 1828.

Beryllium remained a specialist metal. Its stiffness and low density later made it a structural material in aerospace and in X-ray windows, always with care, because the dust is toxic.

elements.history:
Borax was known in antiquity as a flux. In 1808 Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Louis Jacques Thénard, and Humphry Davy working separately, reduced boron compounds and obtained an impure element. Henri Moissan prepared a much purer sample later in the century.

The name comes from borax, itself from the Arabic buraq. Boron’s electron-deficient bonding, and the contrast between boric acid and the boranes, became a set piece of inorganic chemistry.

discovery.text: Known as charcoal, soot, and diamond long before it was an element.

elements.history:
Charcoal, soot, and diamond were known long before anyone called them one element. In 1772 Lavoisier burned a diamond in oxygen and obtained the same gas as from burning charcoal, which tied the forms together. The name carbon is from the Latin carbo, coal.

The nineteenth century sorted the allotropes. Graphite, diamond, and later fullerenes and graphene are the same element in different networks, and organic chemistry is the chemistry of its chains.

discovery.text: Isolated as the gas left after oxygen and carbon dioxide were removed from air.

elements.history:
Daniel Rutherford isolated a gas in 1772 by removing oxygen and carbon dioxide from air and found that what remained would not support life or flame. He called it noxious air. Jean-Antoine Chaptal named it nitrogen in 1790. The French name azote, from Greek for lifeless, is still the root of nitride and azo.

Nitrogen’s triple bond kept the atmosphere’s main gas inert until the Haber–Bosch process, industrialized in the 1910s, fixed it as ammonia. That single reaction remade fertilizer and explosives.

elements.history:
Carl Wilhelm Scheele prepared oxygen around 1772, and Joseph Priestley published the same gas in 1774 after heating mercuric oxide. Lavoisier overthrew the phlogiston story with it and named it oxygen, meaning acid-former, because he wrongly thought every acid contained it.

The name stuck even after that theory did not. Oxygen became the reference for combustion, respiration, and the oxide minerals that make up most of the crust.

elements.history:
Fluorspar was used as a flux for centuries, and the name fluorine comes from the Latin fluere, to flow. Chemists suspected an element in hydrofluoric acid long before anyone could isolate it. Several were poisoned in the attempt. Henri Moissan succeeded in 1886 by electrolyzing potassium hydrogen fluoride in a platinum cell.

Fluorine is the most electronegative element, and for decades it had almost no compounds except fluorides. The xenon fluorides of the 1960s were the surprise that opened noble-gas chemistry.

discovery.text: Isolated from liquefied air after argon and krypton.

elements.history:

Georges Claude turned that glow into commercial lighting in the 1910s. Neon signs made the element a public word, even when later tubes used other gases for other colors.

elements.history:
Soda and salt are ancient. Humphry Davy isolated the metal in 1807 by electrolyzing molten caustic soda, a few days after he had isolated potassium. Sodium stayed a laboratory metal because it reacts violently with water. Its ion, not the metal, is the everyday substance: table salt, soaps, and the main cation outside living cells.

The bright white flame of burning magnesium became a nineteenth-century light source for photography and signaling. The ion later turned up at the center of chlorophyll.

discovery.text: Prepared the metal from alumina; Wöhler improved the method.

elements.history:
Alum was used as a mordant in the ancient world. Hans Christian Ørsted prepared impure aluminium metal in 1825, and Friedrich Wöhler improved the isolation in 1827. Henri Sainte-Claire Deville’s process of the 1850s made small bars that were still as costly as silver.

Silicon was a chemical footnote until the twentieth century. Zone refining and the transistor turned the element into the semiconductor of electronics, while silica remained the network of glass and rock.

Brand’s white phosphorus is dangerously reactive. The red allotrope and the phosphate minerals came later. Phosphate esters became the backbone of DNA and the currency of cell energy.

Sulfur, called brimstone, was known from volcanic deposits and from metal ores long before it was classed as an element. Lavoisier placed it among the elements in 1789. The name is from the Latin sulfur, of uncertain older origin.

The contact process for sulfuric acid, industrialized in the nineteenth century, made sulfur the starting point of the heavy chemical industry. The same element sits in the amino acids cysteine and methionine.

Argon was the first noble gas isolated from air and the clue that a whole group was missing from the table. It is now the inert atmosphere of welding and of many laboratory gloveboxes, and the daughter product used in potassium–argon dating.

The ion is the one that matters: limestone and marble, bones and teeth, cement, and the hardness of water. Calcium carbonate is the mineral record of shells and reefs.

Scandium stayed scarce. It is the first of the transition metals, almost always in the +3 state, and a light alloying addition rather than a bulk metal.

The Kroll process of the 1940s made titanium a structural metal. Its oxide, already used as a white pigment, is still the form most people meet.

Vanadium’s many oxidation states, and the colored ions that come with them, made it a teaching example of transition-metal chemistry. A small addition hardens steel.

Chrome plating and stainless steel made chromium a household word in the twentieth century. The same element’s +6 compounds are toxic, which is why the chemistry of chromate is taught with a warning.

Manganese became the scavenger added to steel to remove sulfur and oxygen. In the laboratory, the purple permanganate ion is the familiar strong oxidizer of titration.

discovery.text: Shown to be a distinct metal in Swedish cobalt ores, not bismuth.

elements.history:
Miners called certain ores kobold, German for a goblin, because they looked like copper ore and gave arsenic fumes instead of copper. Georg Brandt showed in 1735 that the blue color of smalt came from a distinct metal, the first metal discovered with a recorded scientific claim. The name cobalt kept the goblin.

Cobalt blue glass and pigments came first. The metal’s ferromagnetism and its place at the center of vitamin B12 came much later.

Axel Fredrik Cronstedt isolated a metal from the ore Kupfernickel, devil’s copper, in 1751, and named it nickel. Like cobalt ores, niccolite had frustrated miners who expected copper. Cronstedt showed the metal was neither copper nor cobalt.

Nickel stayed a minor metal until electroplating and stainless alloys. It is also the catalyst of fat hydrogenation and a major constituent of many meteorites.

discovery.text: Native metal of tools, coinage, and wiring long before atomic theory.

elements.history:
Copper was worked in the Near East before 5000 BCE, first as native metal and then smelted from ore. The Bronze Age is the age of its alloy with tin. The name copper and the symbol Cu come from Cyprus, Latin cuprum, the island that supplied Roman ore.

It remained the metal of coinage, roofing, and later of electrical wire, because among common metals only silver conducts better. The blue of its aqueous ion is one of the first colors a chemistry student learns.

Brass, the alloy of copper and zinc, is ancient, but isolating the element was harder because the metal boils out of its ore. India smelted zinc by distillation centuries before Europe. Andreas Sigismund Marggraf isolated it in 1746 and described it clearly enough that he is credited with the discovery. The name may come from the German Zinke, meaning prong or tooth.

Galvanizing, the zinc coating on steel, is the modern bulk use. The ion is also essential in enzymes, including carbonic anhydrase.

discovery.text: Found spectroscopically in zinc blende, then isolated.

elements.history:
Mendeleev predicted eka-aluminium in 1871, including a low melting point and a density near 6 g/cm³. Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran found the element spectroscopically in a zinc blende in 1875 and isolated it the same year. He named it gallium, for Gallia, France. The match to Mendeleev’s numbers was one of the periodic table’s public victories.

Gallium melts just above room temperature, which is why a warm hand liquifies a lump. It is now a semiconductor metal, mostly as gallium arsenide and gallium nitride.

Germanium was the semiconductor of the first transistors in the 1940s, before silicon took that role. It remains the material of some infrared optics and fiber systems.

elements.history:
Arsenic compounds, especially the sulfides orpiment and realgar, were ancient pigments and medicines. Albertus Magnus is often credited with describing the free element in the thirteenth century. The name comes from the Greek arsenikon, itself from a Persian word for the yellow pigment.

The element’s reputation is its toxicity. It is also a metalloid used to dope semiconductors, and a reminder that a substance known for centuries was an element only once the idea of an element was clear.

elements.history:
Jöns Jacob Berzelius found a red residue in the slime of a sulfuric-acid plant at Falun in 1817. He first thought it was tellurium, then showed it was a new element and named it selenium, from the Greek selene, the Moon, because tellurium had been named for the Earth.

Selenium’s conductivity rises in the light, which made it the photoconductor of early meters and copiers. It is also a trace element in the enzyme glutathione peroxidase.

elements.history:
Antoine Jérôme Balard isolated a dark red liquid from Montpellier salt brines in 1826, after treating them with chlorine. Justus von Liebig had set the same substance aside as a chloride of iodine. Balard named it bromine, from the Greek bromos, stench.

Bromine is the only nonmetal element that is liquid at room temperature. Its salts became photographic silver bromide and, later, flame retardants and drilling fluids.

elements.history:
Ramsay and Travers found krypton in 1898 in the residue left after liquid air had given up its lighter gases. They named it from the Greek kryptos, hidden. A brilliant line spectrum confirmed it was a new element, not an impurity of argon.

Krypton was the last of the classic noble gases from air to seem completely inert. Krypton difluoride, prepared in 1963, showed that the heavier members of the group do form compounds.

Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff, using the spectroscope they had just developed, saw deep red lines in the mineral lepidolite in 1861. They named the element rubidium, from the Latin rubidus, deep red. Bunsen isolated the metal the same decade.

Rubidium is an alkali metal more reactive than potassium. It has little bulk use. Its atomic-clock transition and its photocells are the modern reasons to separate it.

elements.history:
In 1790 Adair Crawford recognized that a mineral from the Scottish village of Strontian was not barium ore. Thomas Charles Hope confirmed a new earth, and Humphry Davy isolated the metal in 1808. The name strontium kept the village.

The crimson flame of strontium salts became a firework color. The fission product strontium-90, which follows calcium into bone, made the element a public word again in the nuclear age.

elements.history:
Johan Gadolin examined a black mineral from Ytterby, Sweden, in 1794 and separated a new earth, yttria. The metal yttrium was isolated much later. The village of Ytterby went on to lend its name to ytterbium, terbium, and erbium as well.

Yttrium behaves like a heavy lanthanide even though it sits above them in group 3. Yttrium aluminum garnet became a laser host, and yttrium barium copper oxide was the first superconductor to work above the boiling point of nitrogen.

elements.history:
Martin Heinrich Klaproth identified a new earth in the gem zircon in 1789 and named it zirconium, from the mineral. Jöns Jacob Berzelius isolated an impure metal in 1824. A ductile metal came only with the iodide process in the twentieth century.

Zirconium’s oxide is a refractory ceramic. The metal’s low neutron capture made it the cladding of water-cooled reactor fuel, once it could be separated from its chemical twin hafnium.

discovery.text: Found in columbite; later unified with tantalum chemistry.

elements.history:
Charles Hatchett analyzed a mineral in the British Museum in 1801 and announced a new element, which he called columbium, for Columbia. The ore was later confused with tantalum. Heinrich Rose argued in 1844 that it was distinct and named it niobium, for Niobe, daughter of Tantalus. The two names shared the literature until IUPAC settled on niobium in 1950.

Niobium steels and the superconducting alloys NbTi and Nb3Sn are the uses that justified the long argument over the name.

discovery.text: Identified in molybdenite, distinct from graphite and lead ore.

elements.history:
The mineral molybdenite looks like graphite and was long confused with lead ore, which is why the name comes from the Greek molybdos, lead. Carl Wilhelm Scheele showed in 1778 that the ore was neither graphite nor galena, and Peter Jacob Hjelm reduced the oxide to the metal in 1781.

Molybdenum hardens steel and survives high temperature. In biology it sits in the cofactor of nitrogenase, the enzyme that fixes nitrogen at room temperature.

discovery.text: First element produced artificially, from molybdenum bombarded with deuterons.

elements.history:
Mendeleev’s table had a gap under manganese. Claims to have found that element in minerals failed. In 1937 Carlo Perrier and Emilio Segrè isolated it from a molybdenum foil that had been bombarded with deuterons in Ernest Lawrence’s cyclotron. They named it technetium, from the Greek technetos, artificial. It was the first element made by people before it was found in nature.

Every isotope is radioactive. The short-lived isomer technetium-99m, milked from a generator, became the most used radioisotope in diagnostic imaging.

discovery.text: Isolated from Ural platinum residues.

elements.history:
Platinum ores from the Urals left a residue after the platinum was extracted. Karl Ernst Klaus, working at Kazan, isolated a new metal from that residue in 1844 and named it ruthenium, from Ruthenia, a Latin name for Russia. Gottfried Osann had claimed a similar metal earlier, but Klaus’s work was the one that held.

Ruthenium is a platinum-group metal, hard and chemically versatile. It is a catalyst and a hardener of platinum and palladium alloys.

William Hyde Wollaston, working in secret on platinum residues, isolated rhodium in 1803. He named it from the Greek rhodon, rose, because its chloride solutions are rose colored. He announced it together with palladium.

Rhodium stayed the rarest and most expensive of the classic platinum metals. A thin layer of it is the reflective surface of many mirrors, and it is a catalyst in automobile converters.

discovery.text: Isolated from platinum ores; named after the asteroid Pallas.

elements.history:
Wollaston isolated palladium from platinum ore in 1803 and named it for the asteroid Pallas, itself discovered the year before and named for Pallas Athena. He first offered the metal anonymously through a shop, then revealed the discovery in 1805 after a dispute.

Palladium absorbs astonishing volumes of hydrogen, a fact Thomas Graham studied in the 1860s. That property, and its catalytic surface, made it the metal of hydrogenation and of catalytic converters.

discovery.text: Found as an impurity in zinc carbonate.

elements.history:
Friedrich Stromeyer, inspecting a shipment of zinc carbonate that turned yellow on heating, traced the color to a new element in 1817. He named it cadmium, from cadmia, the old name for calamine. Karl Hermann and J. C. H. Roloff found it independently the same year.

Cadmium plating and nickel–cadmium batteries spread the metal through the twentieth century. Its toxicity, especially of the oxide fumes, then pulled it back out of consumer products.

Ferdinand Reich and Hieronymous Theodor Richter examined zinc ores spectroscopically in 1863, looking for thallium. They found instead a brilliant indigo line. Richter isolated the metal, and they named it indium, from indigo.

Indium is soft enough to mark paper and wets glass. Those odd properties made it a seal and a solder. Indium tin oxide became the transparent conductor of screens.

Tin is ancient. Bronze is its alloy with copper, and pewter and solder followed. The symbol Sn is from the Latin stannum. The English word tin is Germanic. There is no modern discoverer.

The metal has a famous allotrope problem: below about 13 °C, white tin can crumble into gray tin, the so-called tin pest. Organotin chemistry and tin plate on steel are the later industrial chapters.

elements.history:
Stibnite, antimony sulfide, was a cosmetic and a medicine in the ancient Mediterranean, called stibium. The free metal was known in the medieval period. The symbol Sb keeps the Latin name. The English name antimony is from the medieval Latin antimonium, of disputed origin.

Antimony hardens lead in type metal and in battery grids. It is a metalloid, and its +3 and +5 chemistry is the heavier echo of phosphorus and arsenic.

Tellurium is a metalloid, rare, and chemically the heavy analog of selenium. It alloys with steel and appears in some solar-cell and thermoelectric materials.

discovery.text: Released from seaweed ash as a violet vapor.

elements.history:
Bernard Courtois, manufacturing saltpeter from seaweed ash in 1811, added too much sulfuric acid and watched a violet vapor rise. The vapor condensed to dark crystals. Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Humphry Davy studied them, and Gay-Lussac named the element iodine, from the Greek iodes, violet.

Iodine was soon recognized in the thyroid. Tincture of iodine became an antiseptic, and the element is the heaviest halogen that is still available as a bottle on a shelf.

discovery.text: Isolated from liquefied air; named for the strange new gas.

elements.history:
Ramsay and Travers isolated xenon in 1898 from the least volatile fraction of liquid air. They named it from the Greek xenos, stranger. For sixty years it was the noble gas that proved the group really was inert.

In 1962 Neil Bartlett prepared a xenon compound, and the fluorides and oxides followed within a year. Xenon is also the filling of high-intensity lamps and of ion thrusters.

discovery.text: Detected by sky-blue spectral lines in mineral water.

elements.history:
Bunsen and Kirchhoff found sky-blue spectral lines in mineral water from Dürkheim in 1860 and named the element caesium, from the Latin caesius, sky blue. Carl Setterberg isolated the metal by electrolysis in 1882. It is the most electropositive of the stable elements.

Caesium melts just above room temperature. The second is defined by a hyperfine transition of caesium-133, which made this reactive metal the time standard of the world.

discovery.text: Isolated from baryta by electrolysis.

elements.history:
Carl Wilhelm Scheele distinguished a heavy earth, baryta, from lime in the 1770s. Humphry Davy isolated the metal in 1808 and named it barium, from the Greek barys, heavy. The mineral barite was already known as a dense stone.

Barium sulfate is insoluble enough to be the contrast agent of X-ray images of the gut. Soluble barium salts are toxic. The green flame of barium is a firework color.

discovery.text: Separated from cerium earths.

elements.history:
Carl Gustaf Mosander, a student of Berzelius, separated a new earth from cerium nitrate in 1839. He named it lanthanum, from the Greek lanthanein, to lie hidden, because it had been concealed in ceria. The metal came later.

Lanthanum is the first of the series that bears its name. Those fifteen metals were peeled apart through the nineteenth century by repeated crystallization, one of the hardest separations in classical chemistry.

discovery.text: Found in cerite; the first of the lanthanide series to be isolated as an earth.

elements.history:
Jöns Jacob Berzelius and Wilhelm Hisinger, and independently Martin Heinrich Klaproth, found a new earth in the mineral cerite in 1803. They named it cerium, for the asteroid Ceres, discovered two years earlier. Mosander later showed that ceria was a mixture and split lanthanum and didymium from it.

Cerium is the most abundant lanthanide. Its oxide stores and releases oxygen, which is why it sits in catalytic-converter washcoats and in lighter flints.

discovery.text: Separated from didymium as a distinct earth.

elements.history:
Mosander’s didymium, the twin of lanthanum, was itself a mixture. Carl Auer von Welsbach split it in 1885 into a green fraction and a rose fraction. He named the green one praseodymium, from the Greek prasinos didymos, green twin.

The separation was done by repeated crystallization of double nitrates, not by a single dramatic experiment. Praseodymium is a typical +3 lanthanide, used in magnets, glasses, and lighter flints.

discovery.text: Separated from didymium with praseodymium.

elements.history:
The other half of von Welsbach’s 1885 split of didymium was neodymium, the new twin, from the Greek neos didymos. The rose-colored salts distinguished it from the green praseodymium fraction. The two had shared one place on the table for forty years.

Neodymium’s later fame is magnetic. The Nd2Fe14B magnets developed in the 1980s are the strongest permanent magnets in common use.

discovery.text: Isolated from fission products; named for Prometheus.

elements.history:
The periodic table had a gap at element 61. Claims from minerals, under names such as illinium and florentium, were not confirmed. Jacob Marinsky, Lawrence Glendenin, and Charles Coryell isolated the element from uranium fission products at Oak Ridge in 1945. They named it promethium, for Prometheus, because it had to be made.

No isotope is stable. Promethium is the missing lanthanide, present on Earth only as a short-lived product of other decays and of reactors.

discovery.text: Separated spectroscopically from didymium earths.

elements.history:
Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran found a new set of spectral lines in a didymium sample in 1879 and separated the oxide. He named the element samarium, for the mineral samarskite, itself named for the Russian mining official Vasili Samarsky-Bykhovets.

Samarium is a lanthanide with a high neutron-capture cross section, which put it into nuclear control rods. Samarium–cobalt magnets were the high-performance magnets of the 1970s, before neodymium iron boron.

elements.history:
Eugène-Anatole Demarçay suspected a new element between samarium and gadolinium for years. In 1901 he separated it and named it europium, for Europe. The spectral lines, not a bulk sample, were the evidence.

Europium is unusual among the lanthanides in forming a reasonably stable +2 ion as well as +3. That pair of oxidation states is why europium phosphors can be both red and blue, and why they colored television screens.

discovery.text: Separated from yttria; named for Gadolin.

elements.history:
Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac separated a new earth from yttria in 1880. Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran prepared a purer sample in 1886 and proposed the name gadolinium, for Johan Gadolin, who had started rare-earth chemistry at Ytterby. Marignac agreed.

The Gd3+ ion has more unpaired electrons than any other simple ion, which made gadolinium compounds the contrast agents of magnetic-resonance imaging.

elements.history:
Carl Gustaf Mosander split yttria further in 1843 and found a rose-colored fraction he associated with terbium, named for Ytterby. The names terbium and erbium were later swapped in the literature and then fixed. The element that kept the name terbium is the one isolated cleanly in the later nineteenth century.

Terbium’s green phosphor line, and the giant magnetostriction of terfenol, are the modern reasons to separate this scarce lanthanide from its neighbors.

discovery.text: Separated from erbia; named for Stockholm.

elements.history:
Per Teodor Cleve and, independently, Marc Delafontaine and Jacques-Louis Soret, separated a new earth from erbia in 1878. Cleve named it holmium, for Holmia, the Latin name of Stockholm. The spectral band was the first evidence. A pure sample took longer.

elements.history:

discovery.text: Separated from ytterbia; named for Lutetia (Paris).

elements.history:
In 1907 Georges Urbain, Carl Auer von Welsbach, and Charles James independently separated the last rare earth from ytterbia. Urbain named it lutetium, for Lutetia, the Roman name of Paris. Von Welsbach’s name cassiopeium persisted in some German literature. Urbain’s name is the one IUPAC kept, with Urbain credited.

Lutetium closes the lanthanide series. With a filled 4f shell it behaves more like a group-3 metal, which is why some tables argue about whether it, not lanthanum, belongs under scandium and yttrium.

Mendeleev’s table implied a missing heavy analog of zirconium. Dirk Coster and George de Hevesy found it in 1923 by X-ray spectroscopy of Norwegian zircon, in Niels Bohr’s laboratory in Copenhagen. They named it hafnium, from Hafnia, the Latin name of the city. It had been hiding in every zirconium mineral.

The two metals are hard to separate, which is exactly why reactor-grade zirconium has to be cleaned of hafnium. Hafnium carbide is among the most refractory materials known.

discovery.text: Isolated from tantalite; named for Tantalus.

elements.history:
Anders Gustaf Ekeberg isolated a new metal from a Finnish mineral in 1802 and named it tantalum, for Tantalus, because the oxide would not drink acid. For decades many chemists, including Wollaston, thought tantalum and columbium were the same element. Heinrich Rose separated the two stories in the 1840s.

Tantalum’s oxide film is an excellent dielectric, which put the metal into capacitors. It is also almost immune to body fluids, so it is a surgical metal.

The English name tungsten kept Scheele’s mineral.

Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal, which is why it was the filament of the incandescent lamp. Tungsten carbide is the hard edge of cutting tools.

The gap under manganese stayed empty longer than Mendeleev expected. In 1925 Walter Noddack, Ida Tacke, and Otto Berg detected element 75 by X-ray spectroscopy in platinum ores and molybdenite, and named it rhenium, for the Rhine, Rhenus. It was the last stable element to be discovered.

Rhenium is rarer in the crust than many radioactive elements. A few percent of it in a nickel superalloy is what lets a jet-engine turbine blade run hotter.

Smithson Tennant dissolved crude platinum in aqua regia in 1803 and examined the black residue that would not dissolve. From it he isolated two metals. One of them formed a volatile, sharp-smelling oxide, so he named it osmium, from the Greek osme, smell.

Osmium is the densest stable element. The tetroxide that gave it its name is toxic and was used, carefully, as a biological stain. The metal itself tips pen nibs and phonograph needles.

The name is from the Spanish platina, little silver. Wollaston’s refining method, early in the nineteenth century, made the pure metal available.

Platinum became the metal of crucibles, electrodes, and catalysts. Cisplatin, a platinum complex introduced in the 1970s, is an anticancer drug.

discovery.text: Native metal of currency, electronics, and ornament.

elements.history:
Gold is a native metal and was gathered before written history. The symbol Au is from the Latin aurum. There is no discoverer and no discovery year. Its refusal to tarnish is why it was money and ornament in every culture that found it.

The yellow color is a relativistic effect: the 6s electrons move fast enough that the reflectivity drops in the blue. Modern use adds corrosion-free electrical contacts to the old uses of coinage and jewelry.

discovery.text: Known as quicksilver in cinnabar; distilled for millennia.

elements.history:
Cinnabar was roasted for mercury in the ancient world, and the liquid metal was called quicksilver. The symbol Hg is from the Latin hydrargyrum, water silver. No modern discoverer is assigned. Alchemists used it for centuries as the supposed principle of metallicity.

Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature and pressure. Thermometers, barometers, and dental amalgam spread it, and the toxicity of the vapor and of methylmercury pulled it back out of those uses.

discovery.text: Detected spectroscopically in sulfuric-acid residues.

elements.history:
William Crookes, searching spectroscopically for tellurium in a sulfuric-acid residue in 1861, found a bright green line instead. He named the element thallium, from the Greek thallos, a green shoot. Claude-Auguste Lamy isolated the metal the next year.

Thallium was briefly a rodenticide and a depilatory, then withdrawn because the ion mimics potassium and is poisonous. The inert pair, which favors Tl+, is the textbook example of that effect in period 6.

discovery.text: Worked as plumbing, solder, and weights; toxic in modern use.

elements.history:
Lead is prehistoric. The Romans piped water through it, sweetened wine with its salts, and named it plumbum, which is the symbol Pb. The English word lead is Germanic. No one is credited with a discovery.

The metal’s density and softness made it solder, shot, and radiation shielding. Tetraethyllead in gasoline, introduced in the 1920s and removed late in the century, is the cautionary chapter. The inert pair makes +2 the common state, unlike the +4 of lighter group-14 elements.

discovery.text: Shown to be distinct from tin and lead.

elements.history:
Bismuth minerals were known in the Middle Ages and often confused with lead, tin, or antimony. Claude François Geoffroy showed in 1753 that bismuth was a distinct metal. The name comes from the German Wismut, of uncertain origin, possibly a corruption of a phrase meaning white mass.

Bismuth was long called the last stable element. In 2003 its only primordial isotope, bismuth-209, was found to decay by alpha emission with a half-life of about 2 × 10^19 years, so the element is radioactive only in a technical sense.

discovery.text: Separated from pitchblende as a radioactive product of uranium.

elements.history:
Marie and Pierre Curie, following the radioactivity of pitchblende beyond uranium, announced a new element in July 1898. Marie named it polonium, for Poland, her birth country, which was not then on the map as a state. They isolated it by following the activity through chemical separations, not by collecting a visible lump.

Polonium is intensely radioactive. A milligram is hot to the touch from its own alpha decay. Later sources were made by irradiating bismuth rather than by mining.

discovery.text: Produced by bombarding bismuth with alpha particles.

elements.history:
The gap under iodine was filled in 1940 at Berkeley. Dale Corson, Kenneth MacKenzie, and Emilio Segrè bombarded bismuth with alpha particles and chemically followed the product, which behaved as a halogen. They named it astatine, from the Greek astatos, unstable. The longest-lived isotope has a half-life of about 8 hours.

No one has seen a visible piece of astatine. Its chemistry is inferred from tracer experiments: it is the heaviest halogen, metallic in tendency, and present in nature only as a fleeting decay product.

discovery.text: Observed as the radioactive gas from radium decay.

elements.history:
Friedrich Ernst Dorn noticed in 1900 that radium gave off a radioactive gas. Ernest Rutherford and Frederick Soddy studied the related emanation from thorium and showed that these gases were a new element in the radium and thorium decay chains. The name radon was adopted in 1923, from radium, replacing emanation and niton.

Radon-222, with a half-life of 3.8 days, seeps from uranium-bearing rock into houses. It is the noble gas people measure for health, not for chemistry.

elements.history:
Marguerite Perey, working at the Curie Institute, found a short-lived alkali metal among the decay products of actinium in 1939. She named it francium, for France. It was the last element discovered in a natural decay chain rather than made in an accelerator.

The longest-lived isotope lasts about 22 minutes. Francium is the most electropositive element, and also one that no one will ever hold: the whole Earth’s crust contains grams of it at any moment.

discovery.text: Separated from pitchblende; intensely radioactive.

elements.history:
In December 1898, months after polonium, Marie and Pierre Curie announced a second, far more radioactive element in pitchblende. They named it radium, from the Latin radius, a ray. Isolating a tenth of a gram of the chloride from tonnes of ore took until 1902.

Radium’s glow put it into watch dials and patent medicines before the danger was understood. The same element gave Rutherford the alpha particles he used to probe the nucleus, and it defined the curie as a unit of activity.

elements.history:
André-Louis Debierne, a colleague of the Curies, found a new radioactive substance in pitchblende residues in 1899 and named it actinium, from the Greek aktis, a ray. Friedrich Oskar Giesel discovered it independently in 1902. The chemistry was hard because actinium follows the rare earths.

Actinium gave its name to the series of elements that fill the 5f orbitals. It is also the parent of the actinium decay chain, which ends at lead-207.

discovery.text: Isolated from thorite.

elements.history:
Jöns Jacob Berzelius isolated a new earth from a Norwegian mineral in 1828 and named the element thorium, for the Norse god Thor. The mineral was later called thorite. Thorium was a chemical element for seventy years before radioactivity was known. Marie Curie and Gerhard Schmidt showed independently, in 1898, that it is radioactive.

Thorium nitrate made the mantles of gas lamps glow white. Thorium-232 is long-lived enough to be primordial, and it is a possible breeder fuel because it absorbs a neutron to become fissile uranium-233.

discovery.text: Found as a uranium decay product; later named protactinium.

elements.history:
Kasimir Fajans and Oswald Göhring identified a short-lived member of the uranium decay chain in 1913 and called it brevium. Otto Hahn and Lise Meitner isolated the longer-lived isotope in 1917, as did Frederick Soddy and John Cranston independently. The name became protactinium, the parent of actinium, because the 231 isotope decays to actinium-227.

Protactinium is scarce, intensely radioactive, and chemically awkward. Aristid von Grosse isolated a visible amount of the oxide in 1927 and the metal in 1934. It sits between thorium and uranium and is not mined for its own sake.

discovery.text: Identified in pitchblende; the metal was isolated in 1841.

elements.history:
Martin Heinrich Klaproth examined pitchblende in 1789, decided it contained a new element, and named it uranium for the planet Uranus, found eight years earlier. He had isolated the oxide. Eugène-Melchior Péligot prepared the metal in 1841. Radioactivity was discovered in uranium salts by Henri Becquerel in 1896.

The nucleus came apart in 1938, when Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann found barium in neutron-irradiated uranium and Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explained the result as fission. Uranium-235 is the fissile isotope. Uranium-238 is 99.3 percent of the natural metal.

discovery.text: Produced by neutron irradiation of uranium.

elements.history:
Edwin McMillan and Philip Abelson produced element 93 in 1940 by irradiating uranium with neutrons at Berkeley. A beta decay of uranium-239 gave a new element that was not the ekarhenium some chemists had expected. They named it neptunium, for the planet beyond Uranus.

Neptunium was the first transuranic element. It showed that the elements past actinium form a 5f series, parallel to the lanthanides, rather than a fourth row of ordinary transition metals.

discovery.text: Produced by deuteron bombardment of uranium.

elements.history:
Late in 1940, Glenn Seaborg, Edwin McMillan, Joseph Kennedy, and Arthur Wahl bombarded uranium with deuterons and chemically separated element 94. The work was classified until after the war. The name plutonium, for Pluto, continues the planetary sequence after uranium and neptunium. Plutonium-239, made by neutron capture, is fissile.

The element was produced in wartime quantity before most chemists knew it existed. Its many oxidation states, and the radiotoxicity of the metal, made it a nuclear material rather than a laboratory reagent.

discovery.text: Isolated from plutonium irradiated in a reactor.

elements.history:
Glenn Seaborg, Ralph James, Leon Morgan, and Albert Ghiorso identified element 95 in 1944 in plutonium that had been irradiated in a reactor. The announcement waited until after the war, in 1945. They named it americium, for the Americas, by analogy with europium just above it in the table.

Americium-241, an alpha emitter with a convenient half-life, became the ionization source in household smoke detectors. It is the transuranic element most people have, unknowingly, at home.

discovery.text: Produced by alpha bombardment of plutonium.

elements.history:
Seaborg, James, and Ghiorso produced element 96 in 1944 by bombarding plutonium with alpha particles. They named it curium, for Marie and Pierre Curie, by analogy with gadolinium, which honors Johan Gadolin. The name was announced with americium in 1945.

Curium is a research element and a target. Heavier actinides were made by starting from curium and adding more helium nuclei, one element at a time.

discovery.text: Produced by alpha bombardment of americium.

elements.history:
Stanley Thompson, Albert Ghiorso, and Glenn Seaborg produced element 97 at Berkeley in 1949 by bombarding americium with alpha particles. They named it berkelium, for the city, following the pattern of ytterbium’s town and europium’s continent. The first samples were a few thousand atoms.

Berkelium’s later public role was as the target for tennessine. In 2010, calcium-48 ions on berkelium-249 made element 117.

discovery.text: Produced by alpha bombardment of curium.

elements.history:
Thompson, Kenneth Street, Ghiorso, and Seaborg made element 98 in 1950 by bombarding curium with alpha particles. They named it californium, for the state and the university. The discovery paper noted that naming an element for a place was already a rare-earth tradition.

Californium-252 fissions spontaneously and sprays neutrons. That made a microgram of it a portable neutron source for reactors, medicine, and assay, and also one of the most expensive materials ever sold by the microgram.

discovery.text: Found in debris from the first hydrogen-bomb test.

elements.history:
Element 99 was found in the debris of the Ivy Mike thermonuclear test of 1952. A burst of neutrons on uranium built the nucleus up many steps before it could beta-decay. Albert Ghiorso and coworkers at Berkeley identified it, and the name einsteinium, for Albert Einstein, was published in 1955.

Einsteinium has no civilian bulk use. It was the starting target for mendelevium, the first element identified essentially one atom at a time.

Fermium was in the same Ivy Mike filter papers as einsteinium. The Berkeley group identified element 100 in 1952 and named it for Enrico Fermi, who had built the first reactor and had died in 1954. The name was published with einsteinium in 1955.

From fermium onward, the amounts are atoms, not weighable samples. Chemistry is done by seeing where a handful of atoms elute from an ion-exchange column.

discovery.people: Ghiorso, Harvey, Choppin, Thompson, and Seaborg
discovery.text: Produced by alpha bombardment of einsteinium; identified atom by atom.

elements.history:
In 1955 Ghiorso, Bernard Harvey, Gregory Choppin, Stanley Thompson, and Seaborg bombarded a tiny target of einsteinium with alpha particles and identified element 101. They used seventeen atoms. The name mendelevium honors Dmitri Mendeleev, whose table had predicted the method of looking for a gap and then finding it.

The recoil technique used for mendelevium, catching the product atom on a second foil, became the standard way to separate a new element from a much larger target.

discovery.text: Produced by heavy-ion fusion; naming was settled later.

elements.history:
Element 102 was claimed more than once. A 1957 Stockholm group proposed the name nobelium, for Alfred Nobel, on evidence that did not hold. Groups at Dubna and at Berkeley made the element in the 1960s, and the Dubna work of 1966 is the claim IUPAC later accepted. The Stockholm name was kept anyway.

Nobelium is chemically interesting because the +2 oxidation state is more stable than +3, a late-actinide echo of ytterbium. The experiments that showed this used atoms that lived for minutes.

discovery.text: Produced by boron ions on californium.

elements.history:
Albert Ghiorso and coworkers at Berkeley produced element 103 in 1961 by bombarding californium with boron ions. They named it lawrencium, for Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron. Dubna reported isotopes soon after. IUPAC confirmed the name in 1997.

Lawrencium closes the actinide series. Its ground configuration is expected to put the last electron in a 7p orbital rather than a 6d orbital, a small relativistic twist at the end of the row.

discovery.text: First transactinide; naming dispute resolved as rutherfordium.

elements.history:
Element 104 was the first transactinide, and the first of the transfermium disputes. A Dubna group reported it in 1964, and a Berkeley group reported a clearer identification in 1969. Each side had a name. IUPAC adopted rutherfordium in 1997, for Ernest Rutherford.

Chemistry on a few short-lived atoms shows that rutherfordium behaves as a group-4 metal, the heavy analog of hafnium, which confirmed that the actinide series really does end at lawrencium.

Dubna and Berkeley both reported element 105 around 1970, from different heavy-ion reactions. The proposed names hahnium and nielsbohrium competed through the transfermium wars. IUPAC settled on dubnium in 1997, for the town of Dubna, where the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research works.

Dubnium is the heavy analog of tantalum. The isotopes last seconds, long enough for a handful of chemical separations and not for a visible sample.

elements.history:
Element 106 was reported in 1974, within months, by a Berkeley group led by Ghiorso and a Dubna group led by Yuri Oganessian, using different reactions. The Berkeley evidence was the one affirmed. The discoverers asked to name it seaborgium, for Glenn Seaborg, while he was still alive. IUPAC accepted that name in 1997 after first resisting an eponym for a living person.

Seaborgium is expected to resemble tungsten, including high oxidation states. The chemistry is inferred from atom-at-a-time experiments.

discovery.text: Produced at GSI Darmstadt from bismuth and chromium.

elements.history:
Gottfried Münzenberg, Peter Armbruster, and coworkers at the GSI laboratory in Darmstadt produced element 107 in 1981. They fused chromium-54 with bismuth-209 and identified the product by its chain of alpha decays. The cold-fusion method they used, a gentle heavy-ion collision, became the GSI route to the next several elements.

The name bohrium, for Niels Bohr, was adopted in 1997. Bohrium is the group-7 analog of rhenium, known from a few atoms at a time.

elements.history:

Copernicium is the heavy analog of mercury and may be unusually volatile. Adsorption experiments on a few atoms hint that it behaves more like a noble metal vapor than like a typical group-12 metal.

elements.history:
A RIKEN team led by Kosuke Morita produced element 113 in 2004 by fusing zinc-70 with bismuth-209, and confirmed the decay chain in later runs. Nihonium opens the superheavy p-block. It is expected to behave like a heavy thallium, with the +1 state favored, but that is a prediction rather than a measured bottle of compound.

elements.history:
A Dubna–Livermore collaboration produced element 114 in 1998 by bombarding plutonium with calcium-48, a rare doubly magic projectile. The name flerovium, for Georgy Flerov and the Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions, was adopted in 2012. Calcium-48 fusion became the route to every element past copernicium.

Flerovium is the analog of lead. Some of its isotopes live for seconds, long enough that it was once discussed as a shore of the predicted island of stability. The half-lives are longer than those of its neighbors, and still far too short to see.

curriculum.advanced: Go further on Oganesson: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; predicted condensed phase is uncertain; teaching, not a sample If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Produced from californium and calcium; named for Yuri Oganessian.

elements.history:
Dubna and Livermore reported element 118 in 2006, from calcium-48 on californium-249, after an earlier 1999 claim from Berkeley had been withdrawn. A single atom’s decay chain was the first evidence. Further atoms confirmed it. The name oganesson, for Yuri Oganessian, who led the Dubna heavy-element program, was adopted in 2016. It was only the second time an element was named for a living person.

Oganesson closes period 7, in the noble-gas seat. Relativistic calculations suggest it may be a reactive solid rather than a gas like radon. No one has a sample. The history of the element is the history of a few decay chains and of the end of the table as it now stands.
